paper_title: NexSight: Verifiable Tasks for Fine-Grained Agentic Long-Video Understanding

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Fine-grained questions about long videos ask how many times an action occurs, in what order events unfold, or exactly when a state changes. Answering them can require finding brief moments scattered across hours of footage. Agentic models that decide when and where to look promise to find these moments, yet this ability is hard both to measure and to learn. Sparse supporting evidence may establish that an action occurred without establishing its total count; verifying timeline-wide claims requires checking for missed occurrences and double counting. Answer-only supervision, in turn, does not explicitly supervise the search for evidence. We present NexSight, which builds verifiable tasks to both evaluate and train agentic long-video understanding. Its agentic pipeline, SightForge, accepts a task only if a verifier blind to the draft answer can reconstruct it from evidence densely reacquired from the raw video and counterexample checks fail to refute it. This yields SightLine, 310 evidence-traceable tasks from 108 long videos, evaluated through SightLoop, a shared multiscale harness supporting temporal exploration, local inspection, evidence integration, and revisiting while recording returned observations. On disjoint videos, solver trajectories on verified tasks become step-level supervision for observation decisions. The strongest model reaches only 54.52% on SightLine, yet 79.35% when given the annotated evidence. With under 6K examples, Sight-35B nearly doubles its base model's interactive accuracy (21.29% to 42.26%), outperforms the 397B model of its family, begins using explicit spatial inspection after post-training, which its base model never uses, and gains over 8 points on two external long-video benchmarks.

Introduction Long videos record how events unfold over minutes to hours, and many questions about them are fine-grained: *Corresponding author. how many times an action repeats, which of two distant events came first, or exactly when state changes. The answers hinge on few seconds scattered across the timeline, which uniform sampling, spreading fixed frame budget thinly over hours, easily skips. Agentic long-video understanding instead lets the model decide when to search the timeline, which details to inspect, and how to integrate evidence across observations [2830, 34, 35], spending its budget where the question demands. Realizing this promise requires two things that remain open: measuring whether an agent acquires the right evidence and uses it correctly, and teaching it to do so. Measuring requires tasks whose answers are correct and whose evidence suffices for anyone to reconstruct them. Fine-grained tasks make this hard in principle: many are global claims, such as count or an order, and proving that an action occurred exactly three times requires negative evidence that no occurrence was missed or counted twice. Grounded benchmarks associate answers with supporting frames or intervals [4, 33], but sparse support alone may not suffice to verify timeline-wide claims, and verifier that sees the draft answer tends to confirm rather than reconstruct it [7]. With unverified references, errors cannot be attributed to missed evidence, faulty reasoning, or flawed tasks, and agentic evaluations, which mostly score answers or milestones [1, 30, 36] rather than the frames actually decoded [15], further entangle acquisition with use. Teaching this ability is harder still: agents must decide where to look next, what to zoom into, and when the evidence suffices, yet final-answer supervision does not specify these decisions. Tool access is not enough: the evaluated instruction-tuned 35B model scores lower when allowed to search (28.06%) than when simply given 64 uniform frames (33.23%). Learning these decisions requires tasks that genuinely demand evidence seeking, answers trustworthy enough to supervise, and records of the search itself; few prior works train on their constructed data [34]  (Table 1)  . Our key insight is that verification is itself an activeobservation problem. Confirming global claim means returning to the raw video, gathering dense evidence where 1 the claim lives, and searching where counterexamples could hide. These are the same observation decisions we want agents to learn. pipeline that annotates from fixed view cannot do this; an agentic one can. The resulting verified tasks serve as both yardstick and training ground: their evidence certifies references and measures what agents observe, and on held-out videos they demand the very evidence seeking we aim to teach. We build NexSight on this insight (Figure 1). SightForge constructs verifiable tasks for two paths: SightLine supports fine-grained evaluation through SightLoops budgeted, multiscale observation interface; separately constructed training tasks provide QA supervision and support solver-trajectory collection. Solvers operate without reference answers or annotated evidence. Their interaction records complement QA supervision for post-training Sight-35B, connecting reliable task construction with both the evaluation and learning of active observation. Evaluation shows that SightLine is far from solved: the strongest configuration reaches only 54.52%, yet 79.35% when given the annotated evidence, making acquisition key bottleneck. At an identical frame budget, agentic window selection doubles temporal evidence recall over fixed windows (19.84%40.63%), yet cross-window counting and state change do not improve: finding the right moments is not enough without integrating them. Training teaches this behavior. Sight-35B raises interactive accuracy from 21.29% to 42.26%, overtaking the instruction-tuned model by 14.19 points and every configuration of the 397B model of its family. Its largest gains come on cross-window counting (+37.50) and state change (+35.19), precisely where better window selection alone did not help, and it begins using explicit spatial inspection after post-training (0.72 calls per trajectory), which its base model never uses. The gains transfer: +8.22 points on Video-MME Long (+9.33 on training-disjoint videos) and +8.13 on an LVBench subset. Our contributions are threefold: (1) Verifiable task construction. SightForge separates task proposals from acceptance through dense rawvideo evidence acquisition, answer-hidden verification, independent review, and counterexample checks, yielding SightLine, six-capability benchmark with traceable visual evidence (Secs. 3 and 5). (2) Observation-level evaluation. SightLoop couples temporal exploration, local inspection, evidence integration, and revisiting through shared raw-video interface under explicit budgets. This multiscale harness records observations, answers, and resource use for joint analysis of evidence acquisition and task outcomes (Secs. 4 and 6). tories collected separately on verified training tasks. The resulting Sight-35B improves interactive performance and transfers to external long-video evaluation sets (Secs. 5.4 and 6.4). 2. Related Work Fixed-input long-video understanding. Video-MME, LongVideoBench, and LVBench evaluate diverse video content, long-context referring reasoning, and extremely long videos, respectively [10, 27, 31]. EgoSchema emphasizes extended temporal reasoning, HourVideo hour-long perception and reasoning, and MLVU diverse long-video tasks [3, 17, 40]. MVBench and Perception Test provide skill-level evaluation [14, 22], complemented by temporaldetail and cross-time diagnostics [2, 5, 16]. LongVA extends language context to accommodate more video frames [38]. Active and agentic video understanding. Wang et al.'s VideoAgent, VideoTree, and Active Video Perception develop iterative or query-adaptive video observation [2830]. Fan et al.'s VideoAgent adds event/object memory [8]; T* targets efficient keyframe search [35]. LongVT couples global previews with native video cropping; VideoSIAH supports evidence-sparse QA and tool-integrated training [34]. Image-based methods offer complementary mechanisms: V* guides visual search, Visual CoT supplies regional supervision, and VLM-R3 trains interleaved region selection and reasoning [13, 25, 32]. ReXTime and VideoEspresso construct video-reasoning supervision [5, 11], while Video-R1 and VideoRFT combine supervised reasoning data with reinforcement learning [9, 26]. Agentic and evidence-grounded video evaluation. NExT-GQA and CG-Bench evaluate answer grounding [4, 33], while MINERVA diagnoses intermediate reasoning errors [18]. LongVidSearch evaluates multi-hop retrieval planning, while VideoGAIA studies toolaugmented video assistance [36, 37]. AgentVidBench evaluates multi-hop video reasoning with tool-agnostic evidence milestones [1]. TRACE / VES-Bench jointly audits decoded-frame coverage and answer correctness for ordering and counting [15]. Full-Video Indexing and Randomized Observation Stratified randomized observations cover the full timeline so that candidate generation does not depend on fixed uniform sampling locations. An observation model extracts visible information from timestamped storyboards; deterministic temporal organization and redundancy compression produce timeline summary without further freeform model rewriting. The summary guides proposals and search; final evidence is acquired from the raw video. 5.2. Task Generation and Dense Evidence Acquisition Candidate generation proposes question, draft answer, and evidence plan; verification requires returning to the raw video. The agent reacquires dense evidence from target windows and assembles chronological multi-frame Evidence Panels that preserve local changes and temporal order. Evidence acquisition is task-dependent: boundary tasks retain views before and after transition; counting tasks cover the specified scope and counting units; identity tasks preserve cross-window identity anchors; and text-related tasks check readability across neighboring frames. Limitations While NexSight advances verifiable evaluation and training for agentic long-video understanding, several limitations remain. First, SightLine focuses on visual evidence and onscreen text across 310 tasks from 108 videos; incorporating audio-visual cross-modal verification and scaling to larger video pools are promising directions for future work. Second, our temporal frame-hit metric (Rhit) measures whether decoded frames intersect annotated intervals, which diagnoses temporal localization but does not guarantee that finegrained spatial details are resolved; combining temporal hit with spatial grounding metrics would further refine trajectory diagnosis. Finally, while our combined QA and trajectory post-training recipe yields substantial gains, future work should isolate the relative contributions of QA supervision and step-level tool imitation under matched training budgets, and investigate whether reinforcement learning provides further gains. 8. Conclusion We presented NexSight for defining, evaluating, and improving fine-grained agentic long-video understanding. SightForge separates candidate generation from raw-video evidence reacquisition, answer-hidden verification, and counterexample checks. SightLine provides 310 verifiable tasks across six capabilities, while SightLoop supports temporal exploration and local inspection under explicit resource accounting. Controlled diagnostics show improved temporal evidence localization, while capability analyses characterize how observation and training gains vary across tasks. Sight-35B, post-trained with combined QA and separately collected solver-trajectory supervision, improves interactive accuracy and external-benchmark scores. Together, checkable task evidence, observation-level evalu8 ation, and targeted supervision provide foundation for studying and improving active long-video understanding.
